stories.headline: Update: Trump Downplays AI Catastrophe Warnings, Citing Need to Beat China
stories.summary:
President Trump on Sunday pushed back against a week of escalating warnings from AI researchers and executives, saying fears of AI catastrophe come from "very negative forces" and insisting the U.S. must maintain its lead over China. "Whoever wins AI, wins," Trump said during his visit to Ireland, declining to directly endorse a slowdown in AI development that major industry leaders had just called for.

The remarks came one day after Elon Musk, Sam Altman, and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei jointly backed a call to slow AI development to reduce the risk of catastrophic outcomes. A former Anthropic researcher, Jacob Coxon, separately told the BBC that employees building these systems are "genuinely frightened" for humanity's future. Amodei and others have argued any slowdown must be coordinated with China to prevent a unilateral disadvantage.

On the legislative front, House Speaker Mike Johnson told CNN's State of the Union on Sunday that Congress would not rush AI regulation, warning against moves that could "smother American innovation." House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries countered that lawmakers need to "act urgently," and former President Obama privately urged Democrats at a Thursday fundraiser to make AI oversight a central plank of their agenda.

The debate reflects a sharp divide: Republicans broadly favor allowing industry to self-regulate while preserving U.S. competitiveness, while Democrats and some GOP governors argue government must have a seat at the table. The standoff leaves Washington without a clear legislative path even as AI companies themselves are calling for guardrails.

stories.headline: Jeffries Declines to Rule Out Trump Impeachment if Democrats Win House
stories.summary:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said Sunday he has not ruled out pursuing President Trump's impeachment if Democrats reclaim the House in November's midterm elections. "No, we haven't ruled anything in and we haven't ruled anything out in terms of impeachment," Jeffries told ABC's George Stephanopoulos on "This Week," stopping short of a commitment while keeping the option open.

The comments come with Democrats polling ahead of Republicans by 11 points on House control and with the midterm elections now less than seven weeks away. Jeffries also said on Sunday that AI oversight would be a "high priority" for a Democratic House, echoing guidance he received from former President Obama at a private Thursday fundraiser where Obama called unchecked AI "dangerous."

Republicans immediately seized on the impeachment remarks as evidence that a Democratic majority would prioritize partisan combat over governance. The CBS News Battleground Tracker released Sunday found both parties see the midterms as fundamentally a referendum on Trump, though for sharply different reasons — Democratic base voters are energized by opposition to his agenda while MAGA Republicans cite enthusiasm for the president.

The impeachment signal adds a new dimension to an already high-stakes midterm environment in which Republicans are defending narrow majorities in both chambers. Any impeachment effort in a new Congress would still require a Senate trial and two-thirds vote to convict, thresholds Democrats would be unlikely to clear regardless of House results.

stories.headline: Exit Polls Show Sweden's Left-Wing Opposition Projected to Win Parliamentary Majority
stories.summary:
Exit polls in Sweden's national election on Sunday projected the left-of-center bloc led by former Prime Minister Magdalena Andersson's Social Democrats winning a parliamentary majority, potentially returning Andersson to power after she lost office in 2022. Swedish public broadcaster SVT's exit polls showed Andersson's four-party grouping ahead of Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson's center-right governing alliance.

A central issue in the race was whether the far-right Sweden Democrats — a party founded in the 1980s by individuals with neo-Nazi ties, though it has since moderated under leader Jimmie Åkesson — would enter government for the first time. Kristersson had announced in April that his Moderates would allow the Sweden Democrats into Cabinet if the right won a majority. Andersson framed the election as a choice over whether "a right-wing extremist party founded by Neo-Nazis" would hold government power.

First official preliminary results were expected around 1900 GMT. More than 8 million of Sweden's roughly 10.6 million residents were eligible to vote for the 349-seat Riksdag. Coalition negotiations were expected to follow regardless of outcome, as Swedish governments typically require multi-party arrangements to govern.

The result, if confirmed, would mark a significant reversal from the rightward shift Sweden experienced in 2022 and comes amid broader turbulence across Europe, including a first-place finish for Germany's far-right AfD in a regional election last week. A Social Democrat return to power in Stockholm could temper the influence of hard-right parties in Scandinavian politics.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Announces Removal of U.S. Tariffs on Irish Whiskey During Ireland Visit
stories.summary:
President Trump announced Sunday that the United States will remove its tariffs on Irish whiskey, making the declaration while attending a golf tournament at his family's course in County Clare, Ireland. "I said, on behalf of the United States of America, I am going to take the tariffs off," Trump told reporters at the event.

The announcement came during a broader visit to Ireland in which Trump also said he would like to see a united Ireland — remarks that drew controversy in Northern Ireland, though Trump later called his comments "fairly routine." The golf tournament at Trump International Golf Links was a central feature of his Irish trip, which has drawn scrutiny over the mixing of presidential travel with his personal business interests.

Separately, White House National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett played down Trump's earlier threats to launch a trade war against the Federal Reserve if it does not lower interest rates, saying he did not expect trade barriers to rise to zero but acknowledging the president holds strong views on rate levels. The Fed is scheduled to meet this week against a backdrop of inflation hitting a three-year high.

The Irish whiskey tariff removal, if formalized, would benefit a significant bilateral trade relationship and was welcomed by Irish officials. Critics in Washington are likely to scrutinize whether the announcement follows proper trade procedure, as tariff changes of this nature typically require formal executive or legislative action rather than a presidential proclamation at a golf course.

stories.headline: Update: BRICS Summit Closes With 'New Delhi Declaration' as Iran War Exposes Deep Divisions Among Members
stories.summary:
World leaders gathered in New Delhi for the BRICS summit concluded with a joint declaration dubbed the 'New Delhi Declaration,' but the document highlighted sharp divisions rather than unity. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi framed the gathering as a push for member nations to become 'rule-shapers, not rule-takers,' hosting Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, and other heads of state around a single table — a diplomatic feat given the bloc's internal tensions, including past India-China border clashes and Iran-UAE military hostilities.

The declaration notably sidestepped the most contentious issues. On the Middle East war, it called only for 'maximum restraint' and condemned attacks on civilian infrastructure without assigning blame. The document made no mention whatsoever of Russia's war in Ukraine — a marked departure from previous BRICS declarations — reflecting the impossibility of consensus among members that include both Russia and nations aligned with the West.

Analysts noted the summit exposed a fundamental fault line: China, Russia, and Iran see BRICS as a vehicle to dilute Western influence, while India has resisted casting the bloc as anti-Western, with Modi explicitly stating the group is 'not against anyone.' Veteran Indian diplomat Anil Trigunayat said what India achieved was a push for 'strategic autonomy in an era of war' rather than a unified geopolitical front.

The summit's outcome illustrates how the ongoing Middle East conflict and the Ukraine war are reshaping multilateral diplomacy, forcing nations with competing interests to choose between solidarity and strategic self-interest. Two earlier ministerial meetings this year failed to produce any joint statement at all, making even this limited declaration a qualified success.

stories.headline: Update: Former Anthropic Researcher Warns AI Safety Is 'Not Top of Mind' at Leading Labs as Congress Debates Response
stories.summary:
Jacob Coxon, a researcher who resigned from Anthropic days ago, said Sunday that employees at leading AI firms have 'not enough time' to consider the safety risks of the models they are building, and that safety is 'definitely not top of mind' inside those organizations. His remarks, made on ABC's 'This Week,' came as the AI safety debate reached a new intensity following Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's public call for a slowdown, saying that even one or two additional years before models reach 'critical levels of capability' could 'greatly reduce the risk that something goes seriously wrong.'

The disclosure sharpens pressure on Congress, where House Speaker Mike Johnson said Sunday that lawmakers will not take the lead on AI safety regulation — a position already covered in today's digest. Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries countered that Congress needs to 'act urgently,' and former President Barack Obama separately urged Jeffries at a private fundraiser to make AI oversight central to the Democratic agenda, warning the technology could be 'dangerous' if not managed with a clear plan.

The insider perspective from Coxon is significant because it comes from someone who worked inside one of the four largest AI labs at the moment those labs publicly endorsed slowing development — suggesting the gap between public commitments and internal practice may be wide. Senator Chris Coons said Congress is 'struggling to keep pace' and that managing AI risks will ultimately require cooperation among industry, government, and international partners.

The debate reflects a broader tension: the United States faces competitive pressure from China that makes a full development pause politically difficult, while insiders and some executives are warning that the pace of advancement is outrunning any safety framework. With midterm elections seven weeks away, both parties are maneuvering to claim the AI safety issue.

stories.headline: Charlie Kirk Critics Who Were Fired a Year Ago Reflect on Lives Upended by Social Media Posts
stories.summary:
One year after the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk on a Utah university campus, some of the hundreds of people fired or disciplined for posting critical remarks hours after his death are speaking publicly about the lasting consequences. Gerald Bourguet, a sports journalist, described fleeing his state with his four-month-old after his home address was published online and threatening messages arrived. He said he does not regret what he posted but acknowledged: 'My life will never be the same after this.'

Kirk, who founded Turning Point USA, was a polarizing figure: celebrated on the right as a gifted communicator who brought conservative ideas to young audiences, and condemned on the left for comments on race, immigration, gun control, and gender identity. The aftermath of his killing prompted a fierce national debate about the boundaries of free speech and the consequences of online expression in a polarized environment.

The backlash against critics was amplified at the highest levels of government. Vice President JD Vance publicly urged Americans to 'call out' those celebrating Kirk's murder, and right-wing commentator Laura Loomer warned critics their 'professional aspirations' would be ruined. Some terminated employees have since been reinstated or received financial settlements; others, like Bourguet, have had to relocate and rebuild their careers entirely.

The story raises durable questions about workplace discipline, political speech, and the power of social media mobs — issues that have not been resolved in the year since Kirk's death and that continue to affect hundreds of individuals whose cases have received little national attention.

stories.headline: Update: Fed Holds Rates Steady as Inflation Hits 3-Year High Under New Chair Warsh
stories.summary:
The Federal Reserve held its benchmark interest rate steady Wednesday under new Chair Kevin Warsh, as inflation runs at more than twice the Fed's 2% target — its highest level in three years. All 12 members of the Federal Open Market Committee voted unanimously to hold rates at the current level between 3.5% and 4%, though nine members signaled they expect a rate hike before year's end, a significant shift from projections issued three months earlier.

Warsh, Trump's nominee who recently replaced former Chair Jerome Powell, used his first post-decision press conference to pledge a commitment to price stability. 'Persistently high prices are a burden for the American people,' Warsh told reporters in Washington. 'This committee will deliver price stability.' The FOMC statement cited supply shocks, particularly in the energy sector driven by the Middle East conflict, as a key driver of elevated prices.

The decision arrives days after the U.S. and Iran announced a deal — set to be formally signed Friday in Switzerland — that includes plans to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the maritime route through which roughly one-fifth of global oil supply passes. Oil prices fell to their lowest level since March following the announcement, and gasoline prices dipped below $4 a gallon for the first time since March, offering potential relief. However, grocery and energy prices remain well above pre-war levels.

Markets had widely anticipated the hold, but the hawkish tilt among committee members — with four in ten odds now assigned to a December rate hike by the CME FedWatch Tool — represents a concrete new development. The rate decision is the first major policy action under Warsh's leadership and will be closely watched as a signal of how the new Fed chair intends to balance inflation control against economic growth risks.

stories.headline: Update: Speaker Johnson Says Congress Will Not Lead on AI Safety Regulation
stories.summary:
House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) declared Sunday that Congress will not take the lead on regulating artificial intelligence safety, even as calls for federal action intensified following warnings from AI insiders about existential risks. Johnson made the remarks during an appearance on CNN's 'State of the Union,' rejecting calls from fellow House members to cancel recess and return to Washington to pass emergency AI safeguard legislation.

The announcement is a significant development in the rapidly escalating AI safety debate. This past week, the four largest AI laboratories endorsed slowing development of their most advanced models, and a bipartisan group of House members urged Johnson to convene an emergency session to legislate guardrails. Johnson's refusal effectively shelves any near-term congressional action and leaves AI oversight to existing executive-branch agencies and voluntary industry commitments.

Supporters of Johnson's position argue that Congress lacks the technical expertise to legislate AI effectively and that heavy-handed regulation could stifle American innovation and cede ground to China. Critics, including Democrats and some Republicans, counter that voluntary measures are insufficient given the pace of AI advancement and the severity of risks described by the industry's own executives.

Johnson also addressed President Trump's proposal to send $5,000 dividend checks to adult U.S. citizens, saying the plan would require congressional approval — contradicting claims by Trump and his aides that the executive branch could act unilaterally on a disbursement that could exceed $1.3 trillion.

stories.headline: Republicans Elevate Anti-Muslim Rhetoric as Midterm Strategy, Drawing Bipartisan Criticism
stories.summary:
Republican leaders amplified anti-Muslim messaging at the party's first-ever midterm convention in Dallas this past week, targeting prominent Muslim Democratic figures — including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed — as central villains in the party's closing midterm pitch. Senior GOP figures, including Sen. Ted Cruz, framed Muslim Democrats as a core threat, a line of attack that has intensified as midterm elections approach in seven weeks.

Democrats and a number of political observers condemned the rhetoric as dangerous and discriminatory, arguing it conflates religion with political allegiance and risks inciting harassment or violence against Muslim Americans. The attacks have drawn particular scrutiny given that Mamdani, New York's first Muslim mayor, was already the subject of a petition from 9/11 victims' families over his attendance at the anniversary ceremony.

Republicans defending the strategy argue the attacks are policy-based rather than religious, pointing to Mamdani's and El-Sayed's positions on immigration, foreign policy, and social issues. They contend that Democratic candidates in deep-blue cities and competitive Senate states represent a sharp leftward shift that Republicans need to make vivid to motivate their base before November.

The controversy underscores the increasingly sharp identity-politics framing on both sides of the midterm battle, with Republicans betting that cultural and demographic contrasts will drive turnout in an environment of elevated inflation and continued Middle East conflict. Analysts note that the strategy carries risk, potentially alienating moderate suburban voters even as it energizes the GOP base.

stories.headline: Uganda's King Oyo Buried Amid Succession Dispute and Family's Claims of House Arrest
stories.summary:
Uganda's King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, once recognized by Guinness World Records as the world's youngest reigning monarch, was buried Saturday in Fort Portal following a private ceremony, as thousands of mourners lined the streets to pay respects. Oyo, 34, had ruled the traditional kingdom of Tooro in western Uganda since the age of three and died last month while undergoing cancer treatment in the United States.

The burial took place against the backdrop of a contested succession. Clan elders named TV news presenter Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, 56 — a cousin of the late king — as the next monarch, with Kijanangoma performing the ritual of casting nine coffee beans into Oyo's grave, symbolizing the transition of power. However, Oyo's family has rejected that choice, with his sister Princess Ruth Komuntale stating the late king left a 2022 will naming his young son as successor, though the boy's identity has not been disclosed.

Oyo's mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, alleged that royal guards had been withdrawn from the palace and replaced by soldiers, effectively placing the royal family under house arrest and restricting their ability to receive visitors. The clan overseeing succession denied any irregularity, with clan head Omusuuga Charles Karumasi stating all procedures followed Tooro cultural tradition.

Uganda's Archbishop Stephen Kazimba Mugalu and President Yoweri Museveni both called for unity and peaceful resolution of the dispute. Tooro is one of several traditional Ugandan kingdoms abolished in 1967 and restored in the 1990s under Museveni; their monarchs hold cultural rather than political authority, but succession disputes can carry significant social weight in the region.

stories.headline: Federal Judge Rules Trump's Plan to Halve FEMA Workforce Illegal
stories.summary:
A federal judge ruled Friday that the Trump administration acted unlawfully when it directed the Department of Homeland Security to cut the Federal Emergency Management Agency's workforce in half. U.S. District Judge Susan Illston of the Northern District of California found that DHS "unlawfully usurped the authority" of FEMA in attempting to implement the cuts, and issued an order blocking the directive from taking effect.

The ruling came during an active hurricane season, with the judge explicitly noting that the workforce reductions would hinder FEMA's ability to respond to disasters. The administration had argued the restructuring was within executive authority over agency operations.

Critics of the plan, including Democrats and emergency management professionals, said gutting FEMA's staff during hurricane season created unacceptable risks for Americans in disaster-prone areas. Supporters of the administration's broader government-reduction agenda contend that federal agencies are overstaffed and that leaner operations can remain effective. The ruling is the latest in a series of court setbacks for the administration's efforts to dramatically reduce the federal workforce.

stories.headline: Update: Murder Arrest Made in Death of Tasia Fortune, Black Woman Found Hanging in Mississippi
stories.summary:
Mississippi police arrested 51-year-old Jarques Ratliff, a Black Jackson resident, on a murder charge Friday in connection with the death of Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old Black woman whose body was found hanging from a tree in the backyard of an abandoned Jackson home on August 3. The arrest followed Thursday's determination by the state medical examiner that Fortune's death was a homicide, which enabled police to execute warrants they already had prepared.

Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney described the arrest as "an important development" but emphasized the investigation remains active and additional arrests are expected. Ratliff had an "association" with Fortune, police said, though they declined to elaborate on the nature of their relationship. It was not immediately determined whether Ratliff had legal representation.

Fortune's mother, Christy Spivey, said she burst into tears upon learning of the arrest, telling officers "thank you, thank you, thank you," while acknowledging the family still lacks answers about motive. The case drew intense national and international media attention after Fortune's loved ones insisted she would not have taken her own life. The homicide ruling and subsequent arrest resolve the initial uncertainty about the manner of death that had fueled public concern.

stories.headline: Wisconsin GOP Gubernatorial Candidate Tom Tiffany Survives Emergency Plane Landing in Lake
stories.summary:
Wisconsin Republican gubernatorial candidate and U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany and a pilot escaped with minor injuries Saturday night after their small four-seat Bonanza aircraft lost power on approach to Wausau Downtown Airport and made an emergency water landing in Lake Wausau. Tiffany said the incident occurred following his appearance at a La Crosse County Lincoln Day Dinner.

After the plane hit the water, it began filling and sinking before emergency responders could reach them, forcing both Tiffany and the pilot to exit the aircraft and swim to a shallow area. Rescue crews from the Wausau Fire Department reached them by boat, and both were transported to Aspirus Wausau Hospital with only minor injuries.

"God was watching over us tonight," Tiffany wrote on social media, expressing gratitude to first responders and noting his wife Chris was at his bedside. The incident drew an outpouring of well-wishes on social media. Tiffany, who represents Wisconsin's 7th Congressional District, is running as the Trump-backed Republican candidate for governor against likely Democratic nominee Francesca Hong.

stories.headline: Céline Dion Returns to Stage in Paris for First Full Concert in Six Years
stories.summary:
Canadian singer Céline Dion performed her first full concert in six years Saturday in Paris, opening a sold-out residency at a Paris venue after a prolonged battle with stiff-person syndrome, a rare neurological disorder that had sidelined her career. The residency is scheduled to run for 26 concerts over the next eight months.

Fans began gathering outside her hotel as early as 6 a.m. to catch a glimpse of the performer before she departed for the show. Dion is one of the best-selling music artists of all time, and her return has been widely anticipated by fans around the world who followed her public struggle with the debilitating condition.

The Paris residency marks a significant milestone in what has been described as a difficult personal and professional recovery. Dion had previously announced her comeback with the phrase "I'm so ready for this," and her appearance Saturday was seen as confirmation that she had regained the health necessary to resume performing at the highest level.
